text.p: Two automotive firms merging to create LucasVarity Plc reported results on Tuesday that showed Britain's Lucas in strong form but Varity of the United States hit by short-term softness in components markets.

Former Lucas Industries Plc, the bigger partner, reported a pretax profit after exceptional items of 180 million pounds ($281 million) for the year to July 31. Finance director John Grant said it was "going into the merger in very good shape".
Its sales rose 7.0 percent to just short of 3.0 billion pounds from nearly 2.8 billion pounds in 1994/95, backed by firm performances in electronics and a recovery in aerospace.
However, Grant, the most senior Lucas director moving to a top position at LucasVarity, said Varity's latest quarterly results showed it was suffering from short-term market softness.
Varity's second quarter operating profit, also for the period to July 31, edged up to $52 million from $51 million, which Grant said he considered "OK, but not exciting".
The two sets of results gave fresh ammunition to both sides in what analysts called a strong two-way pull on the LucasVarity share price.
"The view is that the Lucas side was actually quite good, but the Varity numbers were a bit disappointing -- so they gave something for the bulls and the bears," one analyst said.
By 1330 GMT the share price had steadied down 3.0p at 246-1/2p after volume had been sharply inflated by what market sources called one large cross trade between institutions. It closed at 247.
On balance, analysts said, bearish investors who are sceptical that LucasVarity will be able to quickly deliver extra value from the marger seemed to have the upper hand.
The shares have made slow progress since setting a floor at just over 230 pence when the merger terms were agreed in May, while the whole market and other sector stocks have since risen.

"The bulls say the shares should be rising to reflect the prospect of new cost-cutting, opportunities for deal-making, product synergies and so on, but the market has decided to wait and see," the analyst added, predicting a near-term trading range of 240 to 260 pence.
Behind the scepticism is the prospect of stagnant markets for automotive components amid a predicted steadying of world car and truck markets over the coming years.

Grant stressed that Lucas had been able to post solid advances in both sales and profitability despite flat primary automotive markets, and said this had been achieved by selling higher value-added products and from efficieny gains.

His new managing director, Varity Corp's former head Victor Rice, has said these trends can be replicated at Varity and then amplified across the group after the merger, but analysts said the Varity figures suggested it may have a long way to go.

At diesel engine specialist Varity Perkins, for example, where Rice has promised much faster sales growth once the merger is in place, second quarter sales slipped and were still flat when adjusted for currency effects.
Analysts said this performance rang alarm bells, and certainly encouraged the sceptics to await further evidence before giving the merger the benefit of the doubt.

"The caution will continue until the firm can show that Victor's volume assumptions and margin assumptions are more than talk. We've had all the noise, now we await the facts," said an engineering specialist at one London stockbrokerage. ($1=.6401 Pound)
